item.title: Claude Code v2.1.181 and later use Bun rewritten in Rust, improving Linux startup speed by 10%
item.description: Claude Code version 2.1.181, released on June 17th, and subsequent versions now use a Rust port of the Bun runtime, resulting in a 10% faster startup on Linux. This update has gone largely unnoticed despite being deployed in production across millions of devices. Simon Willison confirmed the use of Bun in Rust by inspecting the Claude Code binary, which includes references to Bun version 1.4.0 and Rust source files. The Rust-based Bun runtime is still in preview, with the latest official release being version 1.3.14 as of May 12th.

item.title: OpenAI reduces Codex model context window from 372,000 to 272,000 tokens
item.description: OpenAI has decreased the context size of its Codex model from 372,000 tokens to 272,000 tokens. This change was documented in a recent update on the project's GitHub repository. The reduction affects how much input the Codex model can process at once, potentially impacting its performance or resource usage.

item.title: Skimlane launches a local-first, customizable AI reading assistant for Chrome with auto-skim feature and user control over active sites [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Skimlane has introduced a Chrome extension that acts as a local-first, customizable AI reading assistant designed to automatically skim new web pages using user-defined settings. The tool allows users to disable the feature at any time or exclude specific websites permanently, maintaining user control over its operation. This assistant aims to enhance browsing efficiency by providing summarized content while respecting user preferences and privacy.

item.title: MLB restricts dugout iPad use to block AI-assisted strategy, citing Mets' involvement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Major League Baseball has limited the use of iPads in dugouts to prevent teams from using artificial intelligence for in-game strategy decisions, with the New York Mets reportedly playing a key role in prompting the change. The league disabled custom tabs on the tablets that allowed access to AI programs starting with the second half of the 2026 season. MLB executive Morgan Sword noted that these custom tabs had expanded iPad use beyond intended purposes, influencing substitutions and pitch calls traditionally made by players and coaches. Former Mets reliever Adam Ottavino said the Mets invested heavily in AI software to assist with pitch selection and other decisions, which led MLB to intervene. The Mets did not comment on the reports. The league's competition committee found teams generally compliant with existing rules, and the new restrictions aim to give clubs time to adjust. MLB began allowing iPads in dugouts in 2015 with restrictions, but concerns over AI use have prompted this latest policy update.

item.title: Analysis of Large Language Model Profitability: Comparing HyperScalers and AI Labs
item.description: This article examines the economic dynamics behind profits generated by large language models (LLMs), focusing on the roles of major cloud providers known as HyperScalers versus specialized AI research labs. It explores how these different actors contribute to and benefit from the LLM market landscape. The discussion includes considerations of cost structures, revenue models, and competitive advantages that shape profitability in the AI industry.

item.title: Apple files lawsuit against OpenAI over device-related issues, excluding former design chief Jony Ive
item.description: Apple has initiated a lawsuit against OpenAI focusing on specific device technology and intellectual property concerns, while notably not involving Jony Ive, the company's former chief design officer. The legal action centers on aspects of device technology without implicating Ive's contributions or involvement in the case.

item.title: Moonshot AI pauses new Kimi K3 subscriptions due to high demand, prioritizing existing users and expanding capacity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Moonshot AI has temporarily suspended new subscriptions for its Kimi K3 product after demand nearly maxed out its GPU capacity over 48 hours. The company is focusing on maintaining service quality for current subscribers while rapidly increasing capacity to reopen new subscription slots in batches. Moonshot AI also plans to introduce two distinct membership plans to better allocate compute resources and stabilize user experience.

item.title: Discussion on how task and to-do management methods are evolving in the era of agentic AI [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The discussion explores whether and how individuals have changed their approaches to managing tasks and to-do lists with the rise of agentic AI technologies. Participants share their experiences using tools like Obsidian and Jira and consider moments in their daily workflows that prompt changes in task management methods. The conversation also touches on the potential benefits and reservations about delegating task management to AI systems.

item.title: JustREPL launches a coding playground without AI features to encourage hands-on syntax practice
item.description: JustREPL is a coding playground that emphasizes learning through repetition and manual coding practice without AI assistance. It provides a straightforward environment where users can write, test, and refine code by typing and correcting errors to reinforce syntax memory.

item.title: AIMakeTattoo launches AI-powered tattoo design generator to create visual references and artist briefs for clients and tattoo artists
item.description: AIMakeTattoo offers a free AI tattoo generator that transforms rough tattoo ideas into detailed design concepts, helping clients and artists communicate more effectively. Users can describe their tattoo ideas, select styles, and generate visual references and briefs to guide the design process. The platform supports various tattoo styles and themes, including animals, flowers, memorials, geometric patterns, and sleeves, allowing users to explore multiple design directions before finalizing. It aims to assist tattoo enthusiasts, designers, and artists in visualizing and refining tattoo concepts quickly and clearly.

item.title: Alphabet and SpaceX drive U.S. equity sales to record levels in 2026, with more offerings expected
item.description: U.S. stock sales are on track to reach a record this year, propelled by large offerings from companies including Alphabet and SpaceX. Additional sales are anticipated as Anthropic plans an initial public offering as soon as September, and banks encourage other tech firms like Intel to issue more stock following significant share price gains.

item.title: AI development requires increased engineering discipline as code generation becomes faster and more disposable, reflecting a shift seen in 2025 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The article discusses the evolving landscape of AI development, emphasizing the need for greater engineering discipline amid rapid advances in AI-generated code quality and speed. It highlights how 2025 marked a turning point when AI code generation became comparable to median software engineers, shifting the economics of code production to make code disposable and regenerable. The author reflects on the skepticism that initially surrounded AI-generated code and explains that the current challenge lies in adapting engineering practices to this new reality. The piece draws parallels to past shifts in infrastructure management and stresses the importance of shared understanding and rigorous validation in AI system development to ensure reliability and safety.

item.title: Report: AI agent bottlenecks have shifted from model limitations to context layer infrastructure, affecting reliability and performance [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: Recent analysis indicates that the main constraint for AI agents is no longer the underlying model but the context layer that manages and structures information for the model. This context layer includes how raw data is compiled into structured, queryable formats and how tools are integrated and retrieved, which significantly impacts AI agent reliability and effectiveness. Experts highlight that many AI systems still connect models directly to raw data sources without an intermediate compilation step, leading to noisy and unreliable outputs. Building a dedicated infrastructure that compiles organizational data into structured knowledge bases and improves tool retrieval is more challenging but essential for agents to operate accurately within real-world organizational contexts. This shift implies that future improvements in AI agent performance will depend more on developing sophisticated context management and retrieval systems rather than solely on advancing model capabilities. Teams focusing on infrastructure around models may achieve better reliability and practical utility in AI agents.

item.title: Individual tests 11 AI agents on venture capital tasks, finds AI excels at data sourcing but struggles with competitor mapping [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: An individual experimented with 11 AI agents to perform venture capital analyst tasks, including deal sourcing and competitor mapping, to evaluate AI's capabilities in professional workflows. The experiment revealed that while AI agents performed moderately well in sourcing startups founded recently with specific criteria, they struggled significantly with competitor mapping, a task requiring nuanced judgment. The benchmark showed AI agents scoring between 55% and 72% in deal sourcing but mostly below 45% in competitor mapping, highlighting AI's limitations in tasks involving subjective decisions. The individual concluded that AI currently serves best as an augmentation tool for routine data gathering rather than a replacement for human judgment in complex analysis, emphasizing the need to test AI models on specific workflows rather than relying on general performance claims.

item.title: AhaPrompt launches free, curated prompt library for AI image, video, and music generation covering 20 models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: AhaPrompt has introduced a free, curated library of prompts designed for AI-generated images, videos, and music, supporting 20 different AI models. The resource allows users to browse, filter, and copy paste-ready prompts with parameters included, facilitating creative content generation without the need for prompt engineering. The platform supports various media types and integrates with tools like Google AI Studio, Sora, and Suno. It offers community-curated prompts across popular categories and styles, aiming to streamline the creative process for multi-model AI users. AhaPrompt is free to use without requiring an account and encourages users to share successful results back to the community.

item.title: Samuel Cardillo launches the Neutrality Project to quantify political biases in AI systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Samuel Cardillo, a technologist and former CTO of RTFKT acquired by Nike, has initiated the Neutrality Project to measure and analyze political influences within artificial intelligence. The project aims to provide tools and insights into AI adoption and ethics by making the politics inside AI systems measurable. Cardillo's background includes extensive experience in building and securing technology systems, including work at Google, and he focuses on experimenting with AI models and ethical AI deployment.

item.title: Christopher Nolan calls AI a transparent Trojan horse widely recognized as a threat amid public skepticism [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Christopher Nolan, director of the new film The Odyssey, described AI as a "transparent Trojan horse" that everyone knows contains hidden dangers, reflecting widespread public skepticism especially among young people. He emphasized the importance of skepticism toward both the technology and the motives behind it to ensure its responsible use. Nolan highlighted the rapid advancement of AI and the strong rejection it faces, noting that young audiences often dismiss AI-generated content as low quality. He also connected his cautious stance on AI to his broader techno-skepticism, contrasting it with his embrace of film technology and his resistance to digital imaging systems. Nolan's comments come amid ongoing industry concerns about AI's impact on creative professions and recent contract negotiations securing protections against generative AI for directors.

item.title: Current AI nonprofit builds open, multilingual AI infrastructure to preserve global languages and cultures, backed by $400 million in public-private funding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Current AI, a nonprofit founded in 2025, is developing open-source AI tools that support hundreds of languages and cultures, aiming to create a public alternative to private AI systems. Its projects include an offline device running AI in 22 Indian languages and grants supporting language and cultural preservation in Kenya, Lebanon, and the Brazilian Amazon. The organization operates as a public-private partnership funded by governments and foundations, including $100 million from the French government and contributions from DeepMind and Salesforce. Current AI emphasizes community control over data and consent, contrasting with commercial AI models that often use indigenous languages without community approval. Current AI's approach focuses on local data storage and collaborative development to ensure AI respects cultural identities and knowledge transmission. Its work highlights the importance of accessible AI for underserved languages and communities, aiming to build an inclusive AI ecosystem akin to the early World Wide Web.

item.title: Webflow integrates AI into security detection and response, enabling a small engineer-led team to handle increased alerts without a traditional SOC [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Webflow has integrated AI into its security detection and response workflows, replacing the traditional Security Operations Center (SOC) model with a small team of security engineers. The AI assists by enriching alert context, automating triage of false positives, and supporting complex investigations, allowing the team to manage a 200% increase in detections efficiently. The AI system prepares alerts with relevant data and preliminary severity assessments before human review, saving over 500 hours in a quarter. Large language models help reduce cognitive load during investigations by summarizing logs and suggesting next steps, while engineers retain full decision-making authority. This approach improves investigation quality and speeds triage without compromising auditability or control.

item.title: Spotify removes over 75 million AI-generated spam tracks but faces artist backlash over inaccurate AI song summaries [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Spotify has removed more than 75 million low-quality AI-generated tracks from its platform in the past year as it battles a surge of spammy content infiltrating playlists and charts. Despite these efforts, the company continues to integrate AI features like AI-generated playlists and an AI "DJ," including a beta feature called "About the Song" that provides AI-powered summaries of songs using third-party sources. Artist Lorde publicly criticized the "About the Song" feature for inaccurately summarizing one of her songs, highlighting how the AI summary misattributed a performance detail based on an erroneous review. Spotify acknowledged the issue and said it acts quickly to correct inaccuracies, emphasizing that the feature is still in beta. This situation illustrates Spotify's ongoing challenge of balancing the removal of AI-generated spam with the incorporation of AI tools that can sometimes misrepresent artists' work.

item.title: Why Andreessen Horowitz's New Investor Left Apple [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Welcome, Weekenders! In this newsletter: • The Big Read: Trump's AI agenda collides with reality • Tech Culture: Welcome to the great private jet drought • Plus, Recommendations-our weekly pop culture picks: "Gastronomics," "Catch the Devil" and "The Invite" At the dawn of the AI boom, the technology sparked a real melee between newcomer startups and the industry's established giants. A good amount of the energy in that fight seems to have diminished lately, with the contest appearing to turn into a slugfest between a handful of heavyweights: Google, Anthropic and OpenAI in the lead, trailed by a few other contenders, like Meta Platforms and SpaceXAI. So that's it-the biggies will grab all the laurels? It's an outcome that has looked increasingly probable to me. Josh Elman, a longtime tech investor and executive, couldn't disagree more. And so staunch is his belief in a forthcoming boom in consumer AI startups that he jumped ship a few weeks ago from working on Apple's AI revamp to take up consumer investing at Andreessen Horowitz. Elman knows what he's getting into: Before Apple, he was a longtime Greylock partner, where he led its investments in companies like Discord, Musical.ly, the predecessor company of TikTok, and Meerkat, which became Houseparty before Epic Games bought it. And before Greylock, he worked at LinkedIn, Facebook and Twitter. To rebut my pessimism, Elman likened the current moment to the dot-com era's early days. "On the consumer adoption of AI, we're still back in 1995-maybe 1996," he said. My conversation with him, which has been edited for clarity and length, is below. First things first, I need to ask: Will Siri actually work now? Yes [laughs]. I think people have always wanted Siri just to be the thing that understands them and can help them just get stuff done on their device. I think it does great at that now. If you're gonna comp Siri to Claude Cowork and try to ask it: "Make me a crazy presentation on blah-blah-blah-blah," like, no-Siri's not designed to do that at this time. But if you do things like ask, "Call that Abe I was texting this morning," that works. And I do it all the time because I forget people's last names all the time. And here's another example: I was driving to dinner, and I was coming to Palo Alto, getting off at an exit, and there's two ways to go. I asked, "Navigate me to dinner with John." And then it took me right to the restaurant-even though I hadn't put the location on my calendar. We'd just texted about it. So why leave Apple now? AI seems to just be getting interesting there. What made you want to return to venture capital-and specifically to do consumer startups? When I left Greylock in 2020, I thought, "Consumer is dead. I don't know if you can do that anymore." And there have been a few companies, like Whatnot, which is an Andreessen company, and Suno. But there haven't been that many consumer AI companies. And the common wisdom has been that OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and the model companies are going to define everything that's interesting in the next 10 years. What makes you so confident in defying that common wisdom? When OpenClaw came out six, seven months ago, I was like, "Oh, I get it again." The number of products that agentic AI can reinvent is going to lead to a Cambrian explosion that hasn't happened yet in consumer. And I think now's the window-now's the time. But I think of the OpenClaw craze as being pretty focused on a small, very Silicon Valley insider crowd who built work tools using it. Of all the amazing examples of OpenClaw use that were shared with me, I think about Claire Vo and Jesse Genet, who are moms who have been talking about how they use OpenClaw to manage their families and their kids. [Vo is the founder of ChatPRD; Genet is the CEO and co-founder of Lumi.com.] In the next six months, I think we're going to see the embers of exciting things coming out in consumer AI. I don't know exactly which ones will pop first. But two years from now, we're going to start to see things that are, you know, a set of agents that help you manage your life, and you'll be able to fine-tune them to accomplish what you want. Sure, consumer agents have real appeal. Won't the biggest companies with their established, giant relationships with consumers-Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, even Apple-just dominate that, too, though? Whether it's finance, travel, health-yes, a lot of us are already turning to ChatGPT or, like, Doctor Google. But there are going to be products that are much richer and much more experiential. And they're going to come from more than just those big players. If a startup was trying to say, "I'm going to be the primary coding assistant," well, that's a category that's fairly competitive now. There's at least five of them. But for travel, there certainly isn't anything yet. One of the things I learned at Apple is: No matter how ambitious and big you are as a company, you can only do a number of things well. And you would rather do a number of things really, really, really well rather than try to do all the things. At some point, that gap between the number of things they can do really well and all the things possible leaves a lot of opportunity for everybody.-Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com) Weekend's Latest Stories The Big Read Trump's AI Agenda Collides With Reality How staff turnover, turf battles and clashing views have derailed the administration's anti-regulation vision. Tech Culture Private Jets Are Scarce. Blame the Gusher of AI Wealth Silicon Valley's enormous surge in riches has turbocharged the market for new and used planes, energizing startups that offer innovative ways to gain access to an aircraft. Listening: "Gastronomics" Alex Mayyasi, host of "Gastronomics," a new podcast about food, business and the business of food, comes as finely pedigreed as a Thomas Keller-trained chef. Mayyasi is a longtime contributor to NPR's "Planet Money" and earlier this year turned some of the show's wit and wisdom into a bestselling book. Now cooking solo in his own kitchen, so to speak, Mayyasi has been applying his wonkish curiosity to topics such as menu forecasting, the bargain grocery wars and the internet-altering consequences of the Domino's pizza tracker. I love a chance to rest my mind from thinking about how capitalism intersects with lines of code and instead turn it to the intricacies of private-label Cheerios and the commotion around gochujang chicken wings. As I'd expect from a "Planet Money" veteran, Mayyasi does a fine job of establishing parallels between food companies and restaurant businesses and what else is happening in the corporate world. And I can tell that Mayyasi, who was employee No. 3 at Priceonomics, a short-lived, Y Combinator-backed media startup, is a techie at heart just by how he neatly likened Aldi, the sharp-elbowed discount grocery store, to Quince-you know, the internet's sharp-elbowed discount cashmere store.-Abram Brown Reading: "Catch the Devil" by Pamela Colloff It is an idea as old as Adam and Eve: The devil can take many forms, many of them less obvious than one with cloven hooves. And there was nothing particularly remarkable in the figure of Paul Skalnik, a tubby schlub of a fellow whose down-home appearance belied his prodigious, decadeslong series of cons across the Gulf Coast. (A version of Skalnik would, in other words, make for an engrossing season of "True Detective.") Skalnik was a fraudster, a robber and a covert polygamist: He married nine women, wedding some of them simultaneously. He was also a rat, and he kept himself out of any truly lengthy prison time by constantly informing to the authorities. He bamboozled them, too, and his testimony put four men on death row. Skalnik's indefatigable villainy-and the government's own exacerbation of it-makes for a riveting yarn, one unspooled with great care and craft by Pamela Colloff, who has been telling such stories for "Texas Monthly" for many years. "Catch the Devil" is a chronicle of Skalnik's misdeeds and his life, with Colloff tracking down an aged Skalnik in a Corsicana, Texas, nursing home, urging him to recant his testimony and save the life of one man still facing the death penalty. Colloff's reporting is riveting true crime and a stern, well-documented plea for America's criminal justice system to rethink how it handles informants.-A.B. Watching: "The Invite" I'm often struck by how the same creative impulses animate both Hollywood and Silicon Valley: In each, you can find enormous success by simply improving on someone else's idea. "The Invite," a witty sex comedy directed by Olivia Wilde, who also co-stars, iterates on a story originally from Barcelona-born writer-director Cesc Gay, who made it into a play and then a 2020 Spanish film. (Swiss, Korean and French adaptations have followed; a Dutch one is slated for 2027.) Wilde's version retains the same basic premise: A rather unhip couple tries to enliven their faltering relationship by asking their free-spirited neighbors over to dinner. Wilde plays one of the squares: out-of-work Angela, who is married to Joe (Seth Rogen), a music professor. Their guests are therapist Piña (Penélope Cruz) and ex-firefighter Hawk (Edward Norton), and their ensuing evening together is a night of entendre, horniness and disappointment: Seldom has a botched soufflé been a better-used metaphor. A large portion of the film was improvised by Wilde and her co-stars, a testament to their collective talent for comedic timing. The score, cinematography and editing are excellent, too-establishing a sense of voyeuristic anxiousness, a cross of Alfred Hitchcock and Woody Allen. Suffice it to say, I expect "The Invite" will find itself a guest of honor at next year's Oscars; Rogen, as something like a frumpled, grown-up "Peanuts" character, will almost certainly get his first nomination. A quibble: Most of the plot takes place within the apartment owned by Angela and Joe, but the broader setting is San Francisco. It would've made much more sense to place it someplace else. I find it impossible to imagine anyone in modern San Francisco being so unfamiliar with polyamory.-A.B.

Trump's AI Agenda Collides With Reality
item.description: In January 2025, just three days after entering office for his second term, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that revoked many of the Biden administration's efforts on AI. The order was part of Trump's promise to take a light-touch approach to AI regulation, rolling back what he would later describe as his predecessor's attempt to "paralyze" the industry through its emphasis on safety. Flanked by venture investor David Sacks, who had joined the administration as the AI and crypto czar, Trump scratched his signature on the order and then turned to his new adviser. "That should take us to the forefront, right?" he asked Sacks at the Oval Office event. "Absolutely," Sacks responded. "We got to win." Nearly halfway into Trump's second term, though, his ambitious AI agenda has been upended. The advent of powerful frontier models like Anthropic's Mythos has fueled fears among everyone from banking executives to intelligence agencies that they could lead to cybersecurity catastrophes. Public sentiment toward AI has shifted dramatically amid concerns about the technology's impact on everything from jobs to electricity prices, prompting hundreds of states, cities and counties to pass data center moratoriums.

item.title: Private Jets Are Scarce. Blame the Gusher of AI Wealth
item.description: After Bill Papariella, a Fort Lauderdale, Fla.-based entrepreneur, sold his private jet charter business for nearly $1 billion in 2022, he took it easy for a couple years. But as the number of ultrawealthy continued to climb in the U.S., another business idea struck him: a company that offered fractional jet ownership, like NetJets, but with a service designed as an even more premium product. Last October, he launched Bond, planning a private plane fleet with interiors lined in Loro Piana textiles, custom crystal from French brand Saint-Louis and cabin attendants on every flight. To give Bond a heightened sense of exclusivity, Papariella capped the company's initial membership at around 100 people, who pay between $1.1 million and $3.5 million a year depending on the aircraft. Its members have an average net worth of $500 million, and about 30% of them hail from Silicon Valley-founders, researchers and engineers at companies like xAI, Anthropic and OpenAI, many of them under the age of 34, Papariella said. (He wouldn't comment publicly on anyone's identity.) Flights on a fleet of 20 airplanes will begin in 2027. "The amount of influx we've had from the youth has been something I did not see coming," said Papariella, speaking from a yacht in the Mediterranean Sea recently. "That's only happened over the last two months."
